title: Scale reads with replicas; every write still goes through one primary
caption: Replicas replay the primary's WAL a few ms to seconds behind, so reads that must see your own write go to the primary.

steps.text: All writes go to the primary. A commit is durable once its WAL record is fsynced: this is the ~5k–20k writes/s ceiling.
The primary streams WAL to each replica, which replays it. Asynchronous by default: lag is usually milliseconds, seconds under load.
Read-heavy traffic spreads over the replicas: 2 replicas ≈ 3× the read capacity. Writes don't scale at all.
Read-your-writes: right after a user changes something, read it from the primary (or wait until the replica has replayed that WAL position).

scenarios.name: Primary dies
scenarios.summary: A replica is promoted in seconds, but with asynchronous replication the commits it hadn't received yet are gone.

steps.text: Writes are committing on the primary; replicas are a few hundred ms behind.
The primary crashes. Writes fail; reads on the replicas keep working.
Failover (Patroni, RDS): promote the most up-to-date replica, here replica 1, and repoint writers at it.
Commits the primary acked but never streamed are lost. Use synchronous replication to one standby when that is unacceptable, at the cost of commit latency.

scenarios.name: Edge: read your write
scenarios.summary: A user saves a change and the next page reads a replica that hasn't replayed it yet: their change seems to vanish.

steps.text: The user renames their profile: UPDATE on the primary, committed.
The WAL record is on its way to replica 1, which is 2 s behind under load.
The redirect loads the profile from replica 1 and shows the old name.
Fix: send that user's reads to the primary for a short while after a write, or wait until the replica's replay position passes the write's LSN.

scenarios.name: Risk: connections
scenarios.summary: Each connection is a backend process; autoscaled app servers exhaust max_connections. A pooler multiplexes them onto a few real ones.

steps.text: Traffic spikes and the app autoscales to 60 pods, each with a pool of 20: 1,200 connections.
Connected directly, the primary refuses past max_connections ('too many clients') while its CPU sits idle. Each process also costs ~10 MB.
A pooler in transaction mode lends a server connection only for the length of one transaction.
1,200 clients share ~50 real connections. Keep transactions short: one idle in a transaction holds its connection.

scenarios.name: Alternative: sharded
scenarios.summary: Split rows by key over several primaries (Citus, Vitess-style): writes scale with shards, but cross-shard joins and transactions get hard.

steps.text: Every query carries the shard key; the router sends it to the one primary that owns that key.
Two primaries take writes in parallel: write capacity doubles, and each shard keeps its own replica for failover.
Cost: a join or transaction spanning both shards needs two-phase commit or app logic. Stay on one primary until writes or size really exceed it.
